section.heading: 10.6 Area

image.alt: A diagram of a baseball field with its measurements marked.

figure.caption: The area of a regulation baseball diamond must adhere to specific measurements to be legal. (credit: "Diagram of Regulation Diamond" by Erica Fischer from "Baseball" The World Book, 1920/Flickr, Public Domain, CC BY 2.0)

section.heading: Learning Objectives
section.paragraph: After completing this section, you should be able to:

list.item: Calculate the area of other polygons.

section.paragraph: Some areas carry more importance than other areas. Did you know that in a baseball game, when the player hits the ball and runs to first base that he must run within a 6-foot wide path? If he veers off slightly to the right, he is out. In other words, a few inches can be the difference in winning or losing a game. Another example is real estate. On Manhattan Island, one square foot of real estate is worth far more than real estate in practically any other area of the country. In other words, we place a value on area. As the context changes, so does the value.

Area refers to a region measured in square units, like a square mile or a square foot. For example, to purchase tile for a kitchen floor, you would need to know how many square feet are needed because tile is sold by the square foot. Carpeting is sold by the square yard. As opposed to linear measurements like perimeter, which in in linear units. For example, fencing is sold in linear units, a linear foot or yard. Linear dimensions refer to an outline or a boundary. Square units refer to the area within that boundary. Different items may have different units, but either way, you must know the linear dimensions to calculate the area.

Many geometric shapes have formulas for calculating areas, such as triangles, regular polygons, and circles. To calculate areas for many irregular curves or shapes, we need calculus. However, in this section, we will only look at geometric shapes that have known area formulas. The notation for area, as mentioned, is in square units and we write sq in or sq cm, or use an exponent, such as $$\text{in} ^{2}$$ or $$\text{cm} ^{2}.$$ Note that linear measurements have no exponent above the units or we can say that the exponent is 1.

section.heading: Area of Quadrilaterals
section.paragraph: A quadrilateral is a four-sided polygon with four vertices. Some quadrilaterals have either one or two sets of parallel sides. The set of quadrilaterals include the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezoid, and the rhombus. The most common quadrilaterals are the square and the rectangle.
section.heading: Square
section.paragraph: In Figure 10.106, a $$12 \text{in} \times 12 \text{in}$$ grid is represented with twelve $$1 \text{in} \times 1 \text{in}$$ squares across each row, and twelve $$1 \text{in} \times 1 \text{in}$$ squares down each column. If you count the little squares, the sum equals 144 squares. Of course, you do not have to count little squares to find area—we have a formula. Thus, the formula for the area of a square, where $$s = \text{length of a side}$$ , is $$A = s \cdot s$$ . The area of the square in Figure 10.106 is $$A = 12 \text{in} \times 12 \text{in} = 144 \text{in} ^{2}.$$

image.alt: A square grid with its sides marked s equals 12 inches.

note.title: FORMULA
note.paragraph: The formula for the area of a square is $$A = s \cdot s$$ or $$A = s^{2}.$$

section.heading: Rectangle
section.paragraph: Similarly, the area for a rectangle is found by multiplying length times width. The rectangle in Figure 10.107 has width equal to 5 in and length equal to 12 in. The area is $$A = 5(12) = 60 \text{in} ^{2}.$$

image.alt: A rectangle with its length and width marked 12 inches and 5 inches. It has four right angles.

note.title: FORMULA
note.paragraph: The area of a rectangle is given as $$A = lw.$$

section.paragraph: Many everyday applications require the use of the perimeter and area formulas. Suppose you are remodeling your home and you want to replace all the flooring. You need to know how to calculate the area of the floor to purchase the correct amount of tile, or hardwood, or carpet. If you want to paint the rooms, you need to calculate the area of the walls and the ceiling to know how much paint to buy, and the list goes on. Can you think of other situations where you might need to calculate area?

example.title: Finding the Area of a Rectangle

problem.paragraph: You have a garden with an area of 196 square feet. How wide can the garden be if the length is 28 feet?

solution.paragraph: The area of a rectangular region is $$A = lw.$$ Letting the width equal $$w$$ :
$$\begin{array}{rcl} 196 & = & {28w} \\ \frac{196}{28} & = & {w = 7 \text{ft} } \end{array}$$

example.title: Determining the Cost of Floor Tile

problem.paragraph: Jennifer is planning to install vinyl floor tile in her rectangular-shaped basement, which measures 29 ft by 16 ft. How many boxes of floor tile should she buy and how much will it cost if one box costs \$50 and covers $$20 \text{ft} ^{2}?$$

solution.paragraph: The area of the basement floor is $$A = 29(16) = 464 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$ We will divide this area by $$20 \text{ft} .$$ Thus, $$\frac{464}{20} = 23.2.$$ Therefore, Jennifer will have to buy 24 boxes of tile at a cost \$1,200.

section.heading: Parallelogram
section.paragraph: The area of a parallelogram can be found using the formula for the area of a triangle. Notice in Figure 10.108, if we cut a diagonal across the parallelogram from one vertex to the opposite vertex, we have two triangles. If we multiply the area of a triangle by 2, we have the area of a parallelogram:
$$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {2\left( {\frac{1}{2}bh} \right)} \\ A & = & {bh} \end{array}$$

image.alt: A parallelogram with its base marked b and height marked h.

note.title: FORMULA
note.paragraph: The area of a parallelogram is $$A = bh.$$

section.paragraph: For example, if we have a parallelogram with the base be equal to 10 inches and the height equal to 5 inches, the area will be $$A = (10)(5) = 50 \text{in} ^{2}.$$

section.heading: Trapezoid
section.paragraph: Another quadrilateral is the trapezoid. A trapezoid has one set of parallel sides or bases. The formula for the area of a trapezoid with parallel bases $$a$$ and $$b$$ and height $$h$$ is given here.

note.title: FORMULA
note.paragraph: The formula for the area of a trapezoid is given as $$A = \frac{1}{2}h\left( {a + b} \right).$$

section.paragraph: For example, find the area of the trapezoid in Figure 10.111 that has base $$a$$ equal to 8 cm, base $$b$$ equal to 6 cm, and height equal to 6 cm.

image.alt: A trapezoid with the bottom and top bases marked a and b. The height is marked h.

section.paragraph: The area is $$A = \frac{1}{2}(6)\left( {6 + 8} \right) = 42 \text{cm} ^{2}$$ .

example.title: Finding the Area of a Trapezoid

problem.paragraph: $$ABCD$$ (Figure 10.112) is a regular trapezoid with $$\overline{AB}\left\| {\overline{CD}.} \right.$$ Find the exact perimeter of $$ABCD$$ , and then find the area.

image.alt: A trapezoid, A B C D. A B measures 11 inches. A D measures 13.5 inches. D C measures 31 inches. Two dashed vertical lines are drawn from A and B to meet the side, D C. The dashes lines are labeled h equals 10 inches.

solution.paragraph: The perimeter is the measure of the boundary of the shape, so we just add up the lengths of the sides. We have $$P = 31 + 13.5 + 11 + 13.5 = 69 \text{in} .$$ Then, the area of the trapezoid using the formula is $$A = \frac{1}{2}(10)(11 + 31) = 210 \text{in} ^{2}$$ .

section.heading: Area of Polygons
section.paragraph: To find the area of a regular polygon, we need to learn about a few more elements. First, the apothem $$a$$ of a regular polygon is a line segment that starts at the center and is perpendicular to a side. The radius $$r$$ of a regular polygon is also a line segment that starts at the center but extends to a vertex. See Figure 10.115.

image.alt: A hexagon with its radius marked r and apothem marked a.

figure.caption: Apothem and Radius of a Polygon

note.title: FORMULA
note.paragraph: The area of a regular polygon is found with the formula $$A = \frac{1}{2}ap,$$ where $$a$$ is the apothem and $$p$$ is the perimeter.

section.paragraph: For example, consider the regular hexagon shown in Figure 10.116 with a side length of 4 cm, and the apothem measures $$a = 2\sqrt{3}.$$

image.alt: A hexagon with its center marked C. Each side measures 4 centimeters. The apothem is marked a equals 2 times square root of 3.

section.paragraph: We have the perimeter, $$p = 6(4) = 24 \text{cm} .$$ We have the apothem as $$a = 2\sqrt{3}.$$ Then, the area is:
$$\begin{array}{rcl} A & = & {\frac{1}{2}\left( {2\sqrt{3}} \right)(24)} \\ & = & {24\sqrt{3} = 41.57 \text{cm} ^{2}} \end{array}$$

example.title: Finding the Area of a Regular Octagon

problem.paragraph: Find the area of a regular octagon with the apothem equal to 18 cm and a side length equal to 13 cm (Figure 10.117).

image.alt: An octagon. Each side measures 13 centimeters. The apothem is marked a equals 18 centimeters.

solution.paragraph: Using the formula, we have the perimeter $$p = 8(13) = 104 \text{cm} .$$ Then, the area is $$A = \frac{1}{2}(10)(104) = 936 \text{cm} ^{2}.$$

section.heading: Changing Units
section.paragraph: Often, we have the need to change the units of one or more items in a problem to find a solution. For example, suppose you are purchasing new carpet for a room measured in feet, but carpeting is sold in terms of yards. You will have to convert feet to yards to purchase the correct amount of carpeting. Or, you may need to convert centimeters to inches, or feet to meters. In each case, it is essential to use the correct equivalency.

problem.paragraph: Carpeting comes in units of square yards. Your living room measures 21 ft wide by 24 ft long. How much carpeting do you buy?

solution.paragraph: We must convert feet to yards. As there are 3 ft in 1 yd, we have $$21 \text{ft} = 7 \text{yds}$$ and $$24 \text{ft} = 8 \text{yds} .$$ Then, $$7(8) = 56 \text{yd} ^{2}.$$

note.title: Your Turn
note.paragraph: You want to carpet your bedroom, which measures 15 ft wide by 18 ft long. Carpeting is sold by the square yard, so you must convert your measurements to yards. How much carpeting do you buy?

section.heading: Area of Circles
section.paragraph: Just as the circumference of a circle includes the number $$\pi,$$ so does the formula for the area of a circle. Recall that $$\pi$$ is a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal number: $$\pi = 3.14159\ldots$$ . It represents the ratio of the circumference to the diameter, so it is a critical number in the calculation of circumference and area.

note.title: FORMULA
note.paragraph: The area of a circle is given as $$A = \pi r^{2},$$ where $$r$$ is the radius.

section.paragraph: For example, to find the of the circle with radius equal to 3 cm, as shown in Figure 10.118, is found using the formula $$A = \pi r^{2}.$$

example.title: Determining the Better Value for Pizza

problem.paragraph: You decide to order a pizza to share with your friend for dinner. The price for an 8-inch diameter pizza is \$7.99. The price for 16-inch diameter pizza is \$13.99. Which one do you think is the better value?

solution.paragraph: The area of the 8-inch diameter pizza is $$A = \pi{(4)}^{2} = 50.3 \text{in} ^{2}.$$ The area of the 16-inch diameter pizza is $$A = \pi{(8)}^{2} = 201.1 \text{in} ^{2}.$$ Next, we divide the cost of each pizza by its area in square inches. Thus, $$\frac{13.99}{201.1} = \$0.07$$ per square inch and $$\frac{7.99}{50.3} = \$0.16$$ per square inch. So clearly, the 16-inch pizza is the better value.

note.title: Your Turn
note.paragraph: You can buy a 9-inch diameter pizza for \$10.99, or a 15-inch diameter pizza for \$14.99. Which pizza is the better value?

example.title: Applying Area to the Real World

problem.paragraph: You want to purchase a tinted film, sold by the square foot, for the window in Figure 10.119. (This problem should look familiar as we saw it earlier when calculating circumference.) The bottom part of the window is a rectangle, and the top part is a semicircle. Find the area and calculate the amount of film to purchase.

image.alt: A figure shows a semicircle placed on top of a rectangle. The length and width of the rectangle are 10 feet and 5 feet. The diameter of the semicircle is 5 feet.

solution.paragraph: First, the rectangular portion has $$A = 5(10) = 50 \text{ft} ^{2}$$ . For the top part, we have a semicircle with a diameter of 5 ft, so the radius is 2.5 ft. We want one half of the area of a circle with radius 2.5 ft, so the area of the top semicircle part is $$A = \frac{1}{2}\pi{(2.5)}^{2} = 9.8 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$ Add the area of the rectangle to the area of the semicircle. Then, the total area to be covered with the window film is $$A = 50 + 9.8 = 59.8 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$

note.title: Your Turn
note.paragraph: You decide to install a new front door with a semicircle top as shown in the figure. How much area will the new door occupy?

section.heading: Area within Area
section.paragraph: Suppose you want to install a round hot tub on your backyard patio. How would you calculate the space needed for the hot tub? Or, let’s say that you want to purchase a new dining room table, but you are not sure if you have enough space for it. These are common issues people face every day. So, let’s take a look at how we solve these problems.

example.title: Finding the Area within an Area

problem.paragraph: The patio in your backyard measures 20 ft by 10 ft (Figure 10.120). On one-half of the patio, you have a 4-foot diameter table with six chairs taking up an area of approximately 36 sq feet. On the other half of the patio, you want to install a hot tub measuring 6 ft in diameter. How much room will the table with six chairs and the hot tub take up? How much area is left over?

image.alt: A patio is divided into two equal parts. The length and width of the patio measure 20 feet and 10 feet. The left part of the patio has a table with six chairs. The right part of the patio has a hot tub whose diameter is marked 6 feet.

solution.paragraph: The hot tub has a radius of 3 ft. That area is then $$A = \pi{(3)}^{2} = 9\pi = 28.27 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$ The total square feet taken up with the table and chairs and the hot tub is $$36 + 28.27 = 64.27 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$ The area left over is equal to the total area of the patio, $$200 \text{ft} ^{2}$$ minus the area for the table and chairs and the hot tub. Thus, the area left over is $$200 - 64.27 = 135.7 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$

note.title: Your Turn
note.paragraph: Find the area of the shaded region in the given figure.

example.title: Finding the Cost of Fertilizing an Area

problem.paragraph: A sod farmer wants to fertilize a rectangular plot of land 150 ft by 240 ft. A bag of fertilizer covers $$5,000 \text{ft} ^{2}$$ and costs \$200. How much will it cost to fertilize the entire plot of land?

solution.paragraph: The plot of land is $$36,000 \text{ft} ^{2}.$$ It will take 7.2 bags of fertilizer to cover the land area. Therefore, the farmer will have to purchase 8 bags of fertilizer at \$200 a bag, which comes to \$1,600.

note.title: People in Mathematics
note.heading: Heron of Alexandria

image.alt: A sketch depicts Heron of Alexandria.

figure.caption: Heron of Alexandria (credit: "Heron of Alexandria" from 1688 German translation of Hero's Pneumatics/Wikimedia Commons, Public Domain)

note.paragraph: Heron of Alexandria, born around 20 A.D., was an inventor, a scientist, and an engineer. He is credited with the invention of the Aeolipile, one of the first steam engines centuries before the industrial revolution. Heron was the father of the vending machine. He talked about the idea of inserting a coin into a machine for it to perform a specific action in his book, Mechanics and Optics. His contribution to the field of mathematics was enormous. Metrica, a series of three books, was devoted to methods of finding the area and volume of three-dimensional objects like pyramids, cylinders, cones, and prisms. He also discovered and developed the procedures for finding square roots and cubic roots. However, he is probably best known for Heron’s formula, which is used for finding the area of a triangle based on the lengths of its sides. Given a triangle $$ABC$$ (Figure 10.122),

image.alt: A triangle, A B C. A B measures c. A C measures b. C B measures a.

note.paragraph: Heron’s formula is $$A = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)},$$ where $$s$$ is the semi-perimeter calculated as $$s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}.$$
